title: Left-Leaning Berlin Coalition Talks Collapse, Threatening Germany’s Governing Stability – DW.com Report
body:
Berlin’s governing coalition‑building effort hit an abrupt halt on Tuesday as the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Greens announced they would no longer pursue a partnership with the Left Party (Die Linke). The decision, driven by a growing rift over the Left’s stance on Israel and accusations of antisemitism, has thrown the city’s political future into uncertainty and revived speculation about whether a new administration can be formed before the end of the legislative term.

The breakdown emerged after weeks of “exploratory” talks that were intended to gauge the feasibility of a three‑party coalition following the June state election, in which the SPD emerged as the largest faction but fell short of an outright majority. While the SPD and Greens share a broadly progressive agenda on climate, housing and social policy, they have increasingly diverged from Die Linke on foreign‑policy issues, particularly the Israeli‑Palestinian conflict. Several Left deputies have publicly condemned Israel’s actions in Gaza, a position that the SPD’s Berlin mayoral candidate, Franziska Giffey, described as “incompatible with the city’s commitment to combating antisemitism and safeguarding the safety of its Jewish community.”

The controversy intensified after a recent Left parliamentary session in which a motion accusing Israel of “genocide” was tabled. Although the motion was later withdrawn, the episode sparked protests from Berlin’s Jewish organizations, which warned that the Left’s rhetoric could embolden extremist sentiment. In response, the SPD and Greens demanded concrete assurances that any coalition agreement would contain explicit clauses condemning antisemitism and affirming Berlin’s support for Israel’s right to security. Die Linke’s leadership, however, balked at what they saw as an intrusion into their foreign‑policy autonomy, insisting that any such provisions would amount to “political censorship” of legitimate criticism of Israel’s military actions.

Analysts say the impasse reflects a broader shift in German politics, where the once‑tolerated left‑wing critique of Israel is now meeting heightened scrutiny amid a rise in antisemitic incidents nationwide. “The SPD and Greens are trying to balance their progressive credentials at home with the political reality that a sizable portion of Berlin’s electorate is sensitive to any perceived tolerance of antisemitism,” noted Dr. Lena Weber, a political scientist at the Free University of Berlin. “They cannot afford to alienate moderate voters ahead of the next federal election, and the Left’s hard‑line stance on Israel is becoming a liability.”

The fallout also raises practical questions about who will command a majority in the 158‑seat state parliament. With the SPD holding 36 seats, the Greens 28 and Die Linke 24, the three parties together would command a comfortable majority. Without the Left, the SPD would need to look to the liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) or the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) for support—partnerships that appear unlikely given stark policy differences, especially on housing and climate measures. Some commentators suggest that a minority government led by the SPD and Greens, relying on issue‑by‑issue support from other parties, could be the most viable, albeit unstable, arrangement.

Looking ahead, the SPD and Greens have signaled they will reopen negotiations with other potential partners, while Die Linke has vowed to continue its “independent” policy line. The city’s legislative calendar leaves little room for prolonged deadlock; a new coalition must be confirmed before the autumn budget deadline, or the parliament could be forced into a caretaker mode. As Berlin grapples with soaring rents, energy costs, and the lingering effects of the pandemic, the political stalemate underscores the challenge of reconciling divergent ideological currents in a metropolis that prides itself on diversity and tolerance. The coming weeks will reveal whether pragmatic compromise can prevail over ideological rigidity, shaping not only Berlin’s governance but also the broader trajectory of Germany’s left‑wing politics.
